about.p1: Community boards are the official, independent, and advisory bodies of New York City Government. There are 59 across NYC: 18 in Brooklyn, 14 in Queens, 12 in Manhattan, 12 in the Bronx, and 3 in Staten Island. They vote on issues across policy areas such as land use (first stop in ULURP), landmarks, liquor licenses, transportation, and budgets (past votes and minutes). Members are appointed by the borough president (half) and the city council members overlapping with the community district.
about.p2: This app focuses on Brooklyn Community Board 6 (CB6), which encompasses the neighborhoods of Park Slope, Carroll Gardens, Cobble Hill, the Columbia Waterfront, Red Hook, and Gowanus. Please note that the numbers start over in every borough, so there is a CB6 in Manhattan, Queens, and the Bronx.
about.p3: But like I said, this app focuses on Brooklyn’s 6th community district, but we have apps that go beyond those boundaries if you're interested.

about.sub: What CB6 does, and what it covers
about.title: What is a community board?

items.a: The community board for Park Slope, Carroll Gardens, Cobble Hill, Red Hook, Gowanus and the Columbia Street Waterfront District, home to 120,660 residents (2022 PUMA figure).

Every major land use change in CB6, from a rezoning to a variance, goes through a public review with fixed steps and clocks, and CB6 gets a formal vote in each one. The vote is advisory, but it is on the record and the later decision makers read it. How review works, under Zoning and land use review in the Land Use tab, walks through each process.
items.q: What does the board vote on?

items.a: The Full Board meets on the second Wednesday of each month, except July and August. All meetings are open to the public. Monthly Full Board meetings are held at the Van Alen Institute, 303 Bond Street, Gowanus, in person and on Zoom. The space is ADA accessible. Every upcoming board and committee meeting is in the Meetings tab.

Email info@bkcb6.org or call (718) 643-3027. The office is at 250 Baltic Street, Brooklyn, NY 11201-6401, open Monday to Friday, 9:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m. Email is the best way to reach the board. It gets the fastest response and creates a record for issues like 311 complaints that need follow up.

Report it to 311 first. If it needs follow up, email info@bkcb6.org: email creates a record the board can follow up on. 311, crime, tickets and permits, under Around you on Home, shows the complaints filed in CB6.
items.q: How do I report a problem like a pothole or a missed pickup?

items.a: Who represents CB6, on Home, lists every elected official from the City Council to Congress. The Orgs tab has a full profile for each one, starting with the local officials.
Open the meeting in the Meetings tab or on Home and tap Remind me one hour before.
items.q: How do I get a reminder for a meeting?

items.a: From the calendar on bkcb6.app. The app's copy is rebuilt from it three times a day, and a meeting drops off once it is over.
items.q: Where do the calendar events come from?

items.a: Your block, at the top of Home, or Block cards under Around you: find your street for alternate side parking, trash and recycling days, your poll site and the nearest subway.
items.q: How do I find alternate side parking, trash days or my poll site for my block?

items.a: Tap the Election 2026 card on Home for your ballot, your early voting site and your Election Day poll site.
Open the map from The district on the map on Home. Type an address or place in the search box, or tap a neighborhood or topic.
items.q: How do I search the map?

items.a: Yes. The maps, lots, blocks, minutes and profiles are all on your phone and work without a connection. Typing an address uses the internet when it is available; offline, the search matches CB6 lots.
items.q: Does the app work without a connection?

items.a: The app checks for new meetings and data whenever it opens with a connection. Pull down on Home to check now; the time of the last check is at the bottom of Home.

landmarks.sub: CB6 has 6 historic districts. The Landmarks & Land Use Committee reviews all Certificate of Appropriateness applications before they go to LPC.
landmarks.title: Landmarks & Historic Districts

what.text: An NYC Historic District is a defined area designated by the Landmarks Preservation Commission for its architectural, cultural, or historic significance. Places like large parts of Park Slope and Cobble Hill reflect distinct periods of the city’s history, and exterior changes generally require LPC approval to preserve that character. A good rule of thumb is to check the street signs: brown with white lettering usually means you are in a historic district, while green with white lettering usually means you are not. In Brooklyn Community Board 6, that often means we are part of the review process for applications seeking LPC approval, including Certificates of Appropriateness for proposed changes to landmarked properties.

steps.lyric: And you may find yourself in Brooklyn Community Board 6.
steps.text: Home starts with today’s strip over the district map: parking, sanitation, schools, the subway and the weather. Then the next CB6 meeting and the countdown to Election Day, then your block: type your address or use your location for your trash days, parking, poll site, who represents you and what is happening nearby. The buttons below are by topic: around you, services and business, land use and government, projects and plans. Pull down on the screen and the app checks for new meetings and data.
steps.title: Home

steps.lyric: And you may ask yourself, “Where is my large automobile?” Probably on the other side of the street by Tuesday.
steps.text: The map covers the whole district. You can search any address, jump to one of the six neighborhoods, or choose topics like zoning, parks, schools or transit and see only the layers that go with them. Save your block and your topics, and the map opens where and how you want it.
steps.title: The map

steps.lyric: Letting the days go by, full board on the second Wednesday.
steps.text: Every upcoming full board and committee meeting, with the time, the place and what’s on the agenda. The community calendar sits alongside it, so you can see what’s happening across the district, not just at CB6. A meeting drops off once it’s over, and you can set a reminder for one hour before.
steps.title: Meetings

steps.lyric: And you may tell yourself, “This is not my beautiful house.” Check the zoning.
steps.text: What can be built, where, at what scale and for whom is decided long before anything goes up. This is where you can read that record. Every lot in CB6 is on the map, colored by land use or zoning. Tap one for its zoning, the building and its city records. The Gowanus rezoning and the Brooklyn Marine Terminal each have their own pages here.
steps.title: Land Use

steps.lyric: And you may ask yourself, “Who does all this?”
steps.text: The people and institutions that shape the district: the community organizations, the elected officials from the City Council to Congress, and the city agencies we work with. Each profile covers what they do, where they are and what they have coming up.
